summary: Yes, both spectra show graphene-type sp2 carbon: G near 1580 cm-1 and a single symmetric 2D band near 2680–2695 cm-1, with I2D/IG about 2–3. Both are consistent with monolayer or electronically decoupled few-layer graphene, though thickness is not proven. The Au spectrum is clean, with 2D at about 20σ signal-to-noise (S/N), and shows a clear D band (D/G about 1) that points to a defective or small-domain layer. The Cu spectrum has the same bands but 3–7 times weaker over a lower, strong broad luminescence background, so only 2D is a firm detection and G and D are marginal. The 2D band is about 14 cm-1 higher on Cu than on Au, and the intensity and D-band differences are only partly reliable. I would attribute the difference to substrate-dependent coupling, strain and doping (including thermal-mismatch strain on rapid cooling) and to the very different enhancement and background on the two metals, not to a different carbon phase. The data cannot separate these causes without the laser wavelength and a more careful measurement of the Cu sample.

observations.finding: Au spectrum: clear G, D and 2D bands of graphene on a smooth, broad background
observations.evidence: Single-Lorentzian fits on local linear baselines. G = 1580.3±0.9 cm-1, FWHM 26±3, height 116 counts (noise 16). D = 1344.4±1.1 cm-1, FWHM 34–37, height 110. 2D = 2681.0±0.4 cm-1, FWHM 41.5±1.6, height 344 (noise 20, S/N about 17). The raw baseline is about 1000–1500 counts, so the bands sit on a large luminescence hump that peaks near 2500 cm-1.

observations.finding: Cu spectrum: same three bands, but only 2D is clearly detected
observations.evidence: 2D = 2695.5±1.3 cm-1, FWHM 43±5, height 50±8 (S/N about 6). G = 1580.6±2.7 cm-1, FWHM about 30, height 24 (S/N about 2.5). D = 1350±4 cm-1, height 14, area 439±217, which is only about 2σ. The raw counts are about 620–820 on a hump peaking near 1600–2000 cm-1, with sharp features at the noise level.

observations.finding: Intensity ratios are similar on both metals, but D/G on Cu is not significant
observations.evidence: I2D/IG (heights): Au 2.9±0.7, Cu about 2.1±1. ID/IG (heights): Au 0.96±0.3 (area ratio about 1.4±0.3), Cu 0.6±0.4. A high I2D/IG with a single symmetric 2D of FWHM about 41–43 matches monolayer or turbostratic (decoupled) few-layer graphene, not Bernal bilayer or graphite. Bernal stacking would give a broader, asymmetric multi-component 2D with FWHM above about 50–60 and I2D/IG below 1. The 2D band is about 1.4 times broader than suspended monolayer (about 25–30), which is typical of strain inhomogeneity and substrate coupling.
observations.source: Ferrari et al., PRL 97, 187401 (2006), Figs. 1–3; Ferrari & Basko, Nat. Nanotechnol. 8, 235 (2013), Figs. 2–3

observations.finding: Au layer contains substantial defects or boundaries; the defect type cannot be determined
observations.evidence: ID/IG about 1 with D FWHM 34–37 and G FWHM 26 means the D band is strong. The D' shoulder near 1620 is not significant (residual about 30 against noise 18). If the laser were 532 nm, the Cançado relation L_D^2 = 1.8e-9·λ^4·(IG/ID) gives an inter-defect distance of roughly 10–12 nm. That figure assumes point-like defects in the stage-1 regime, and the wavelength is an assumption. With D' unresolved, edges or grain boundaries (small domains from rapid cooling and wrinkles) are more likely than vacancies.
observations.source: Cançado et al., Nano Lett. 11, 3190 (2011), Eq. 4 and Fig. 3; Lucchese et al., Carbon 48, 1592 (2010)

observations.finding: 2D band is about 14 cm-1 higher on Cu than on Au while G is identical, so the 2D shift is not simply strain or a different laser
observations.evidence: ΔG = 0.3±3 cm-1 against Δ2D = +14.5±1.4 cm-1. Uniaxial or biaxial strain moves 2D about 2.2 times (biaxial) or about 2.4 times (uniaxial) as much as G, so a 14 cm-1 2D shift should come with a G shift of about 6 cm-1. That is about 2σ larger than the measured ΔG. Doping changes G much more than 2D and does not produce a clean 2D-only shift. A combined strain-and-doping change, or different coupling to the metal (screening, charge transfer, hybridisation, local dielectric environment), would fit better. Graphene on liquid-then-solidified metal also goes through substrate contraction on cooling. The shift is the same in both samples only if the same laser was used.
observations.source: Lee et al., Nat. Commun. 3, 1024 (2012), Figs. 2–3 (strain vs doping vector analysis); Mohiuddin et al., PRB 79, 205433 (2009)

observations.finding: The much lower Raman signal and weak D/G on Cu most plausibly reflect substrate optics and coupling, not necessarily fewer defects
observations.evidence: Raw peak heights above the background are 3–7 times lower on Cu (2D 50 vs 344). Au supports plasmonic (possibly SERS-like) enhancement and the Au background is smoother. Cu gives a strong interband luminescence continuum and stronger graphene–metal hybridisation, both of which suppress or mask the graphene Raman signal. The relative ID/IG on Cu therefore carries a large uncertainty. I did not model absolute enhancement factors.

observations.finding: Both broad backgrounds are metal luminescence or electronic Raman, not graphene features
observations.evidence: Au hump spans about 500–3650 cm-1 and peaks near 2500 cm-1; the Cu hump peaks near 1600–2000 cm-1. Their peak positions, in cm-1 on this axis, differ by hundreds of cm-1, which is consistent with metal interband photoluminescence and varies with excitation wavelength. The Cu sample also has structured noise-level bumps (for example at 3026 and 3286 cm-1, below 3σ), which I do not interpret as peaks.

properties.name: layers
properties.value: monolayer or few-layer decoupled (turbostratic); thickness not uniquely determined (single symmetric 2D, FWHM about 41–43, I2D/IG about 2–3)

properties.name: defect_level
properties.value: Au: medium-high (ID/IG about 1); Cu: unconstrained (D/G 0.6±0.4, D at about 2σ)

properties.name: L_D_nm
properties.value: about 10–12 nm for Au, assuming 532 nm excitation and point-like defects; no value for Cu

properties.name: strain_sign
properties.value: not determined. G is 1580–1581 cm-1 on both, so no clear compressive stiffening. Thermal-mismatch compression on cooling is expected but not resolved, and the strain-doping decomposition fails for the 14 cm-1 2D offset.

properties.name: doping_type
properties.value: not determined; G position near undoped values on both, with no G-width or 2D/G-ratio change large enough to assign p or n

caveats: Laser wavelength is missing from the files. Absolute D and 2D positions (both disperse with excitation energy, 2D by about 100 cm-1/eV) and the L_D estimate cannot be interpreted without it. Even if the same laser was used for both, the shift between Au and Cu is only meaningful then.
Cu S/N is poor (G about 2.5, D below 2σ). The Cu D/G, I2D/IG and G width are not reliable. The 2D position on Cu is better constrained but still ±1.3 cm-1.

Single-Lorentzian 2D fits on a sloping background are approximate and the baseline choice affects heights and widths by 10–20% for the weak Cu bands. Peak heights were used instead of integrated areas, which is the convention for ID/IG but is sensitive to line shape differences between the two spectra.

Au enhancement (plasmonic or SERS-like) and Cu luminescence mean raw intensities are not comparable between samples. The absolute intensity differences are not a measure of graphene quantity or quality.

The 2D shift between metals can come from several effects: strain, doping, substrate screening, hybridisation with Cu, or different local strain from thermal contraction after 50 K/s cooling. Doping and strain alone are not consistent with the unchanged G position, but G on Cu is only ±3 cm-1.

Measuring graphene on metal in a spectrum of limited S/N means a monolayer vs few-layer decoupled stack cannot be told apart. Layer decoupling and rotational stacking can produce a symmetric, narrow 2D band in few-layer samples.
Heating at 0.2 mW is probably low but not verified; strong absorption by the metal could shift G and 2D by a few cm-1 through local heating, particularly on Au.
questions_for_user: What was the laser wavelength? It is needed to interpret the absolute 2D position, the D/G ratio and the L_D estimate, and to judge whether Au plasmonic enhancement or Cu interband luminescence is expected.

Were both spectra taken with the same laser, spot size and acquisition time, and is the spot at a single point or averaged over an area? This decides whether the roughly 14 cm-1 2D shift and the 3–7 times intensity difference are real.

Can you provide a map or several spectra per sample? The ID/IG and 2D widths vary across a polycrystalline layer and a single point on Cu with S/N below 3 for G and D cannot show whether it is defect-free.
Was a bare-metal reference spectrum measured on the same droplet away from the graphene? It would separate substrate background from carbon signal.
What are the layer thickness and coverage from other techniques (SEM, AFM, LEED, optical contrast after transfer)? Raman alone cannot establish monolayer vs decoupled few-layer here.
After 50 K/s cooling, was the graphene still on the solidified metal droplet, and was any oxide or contamination (for example amorphous carbon) present? Those would change the D band and background.

limits: Cannot determine absolute layer number, doping level or strain magnitude without the laser wavelength and more than one point per sample.
Cannot assign defect type (vacancy, edge, sp3) because D' is not resolved, and D/G on Cu is below significance.
Cannot say how much of the Au vs Cu intensity difference is plasmonic enhancement, luminescence masking, or true differences in graphene coverage or quality.
Cannot rule out that the 14 cm-1 2D offset partly reflects a different excitation condition, since the wavelength field is empty in both files.
No temperature or magnetic-order information is available from these two room-temperature spectra.
